en: Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Treatise Examining the Object of Cognition) Composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty
Expounded by the Śramaṇa Mingyu of Shu.

"Contemplation" (*guan*) means to examine the meaning. "The object-conditioned" (*suoyuan*) means that which possesses the sense of being an objective domain. "Conditioning" (*yuan*) means that which is capable of inducing the arising of consciousness.

That is to say, when one examines the objective domain that serves as the condition, and it is also capable of inducing the arising of consciousness, only then does it constitute an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus, the treatise states:

The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "It arises bearing that aspect (*nimitta*) and is produced from it. The *Vyākhyā* explains: "In principle, whatever is an object must produce a consciousness that resembles its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That which produces the consciousness corresponding to the object is the producer, and that [object] is the objective support (*ālambana*).

Thus, one should know that the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is exclusively dharmas such as form (*rūpa*), which fully possess both the sense of being an object and the sense of inducing [consciousness]."

Regarding those of other vehicles who separately maintain that atoms [are real]: even if one grants that they can produce [effects], they lack the sense of being an objective domain (*viṣaya*). Regarding those who separately maintain that composites [are real]:

even if one grants that they possess the sense of an objective domain, they furthermore lack the capacity to produce [effects]. Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] causes them to examine whether these two meanings are complete;
only then can a thesis be established.
Regarding those who wish to maintain that the five consciousnesses, such as eye-consciousness and the rest, have external forms as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

some hold that atoms (*paramāṇu*) possess substantial reality because they are capable of producing consciousness; others hold that it is the aggregate (*saṃghāta*), because when consciousness arises, it bears the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [aggregate].

The adherents of other vehicles maintain that mind and its objects are dualistic; they claim that apart from consciousness, there exist external objects such as the five sensory realms (pañca-viṣaya) which serve as the objective conditions (ālambana-pratyaya) for the visual consciousness and the others.
This is not the case for the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), because that mental consciousness only takes conventional constructs (prajñapti) as its objects.

The *Śāstra-vyākhyā* states that the intention of other vehicles is as follows: Even if one were to grant that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has a partial aspect that takes real entities as its objects, it is still able to take a semblance-image of those objects;
thus, the object is not separate from the consciousness. In the case of the visual and other sensory consciousnesses, however, the object is inseparable [from the consciousness].

Therefore, it is known that those [opponents] maintain that external phenomena such as form serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) exclusively for the five consciousnesses, or they maintain...
[The opponent] replies: "No. They maintain that the essence of an atom (*paramāṇu*) is devoid of transformation; this is the meaning of its being substantially real (*dravyasat*).
Since its essence is substantially real, it is capable of producing consciousness. Therefore, they hold that atoms function as the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). The *Vyākhyā* states:

"Or perhaps [it is granted that], although atoms are indeed atoms, it is only when they have gathered together that perception arises and ceases. Nevertheless, in their substantial reality, each one individually serves as a condition."

The collection of conditions is like form and so forth; even if all their respective sense faculties are present before one, the objects do not become confused, because the functional capacity of each faculty is determined.
Thus, they possess the power to discern actual entities.

Each individual atom constitutes an object of cognition, because it possesses the nature of being a cause, and because it possesses the nature of being the cause for those consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness. This is that...

This establishes the sense of being a "friend" (a supportive condition). However, some say that the objective referent (*ālambana*) is the cause for the arising of consciousness because it exists among the various conditions;

they cite this to prove that atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). Alternatively, there are those who maintain that it is the composite (*saṃghāta*) [that serves as the object].
They assert that atoms possess the characteristic of aggregation and function as an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Since an object of cognition must be substantially real in order to necessarily produce consciousness, when consciousness arises, it does so by bearing the aspect (*ākāra*) of that object; thus, they maintain that the composite whole serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The *Vyākhyā* states: "Or again, regarding that which is a collective aggregate"—those theorists maintain that the various atoms [constitute the object].

There is a composite aggregate which serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because consciousness arises with its characteristics based upon that [aggregate]. Since cognition is produced in dependence upon a collective totality, it is certain that this [aggregate] is the object-condition.
As it is said: "If consciousness possesses the aspect (*ākāra*) of something, that thing is the objective domain (*viṣaya*) of that [consciousness].
This is also cited to prove that the synthesis [of atoms] constitutes the object-condition.
Both [positions] are irrational. Why is this so?

An atom, even if it serves as a condition for the five consciousnesses, is not their object-condition (*ālambana*), because the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [atom] does not exist within the consciousness, just like the eye-faculty and so forth.
The Master of the Treatise refutes in general the prior position that the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the first five consciousnesses;

both [theories] are irrational. Why is this so? This interrogates and explains the meaning of their irrationality. Below the section on "atoms," he establishes an inference (*anumāna*) to refute them:
"Atoms" is the subject (*dharmin*) of the prior thesis; regarding the five consciousnesses, even if they were posited as conditions, they would not be the objective conditions (*ālambana*).
Thesis: Because those characteristics lack consciousness, they serve as the cause [of non-perception], just as the visual faculty and so forth serve as the analogy.
That is to say, because the substance of the *paramāṇu* (extreme atom) as it is conceived by them is devoid of transformation, it is asserted to be substantially existent.

Even if one were to grant that it serves as a condition for the arising of consciousness within the five sensory cognitions, it is not the objective referent (*ālambana*). This is because the characteristic of the *paramāṇu* does not appear upon the visual or other sensory cognitions.
Because it is non-existent, just as the five faculties such as the eye do not possess the objective referent (ālambana) within the five consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness.
This is because the eye does not see itself, the ear does not hear itself, the nose does not smell itself, the tongue does not taste itself, and the body does not touch itself.

Thus, it is said that the characteristics of the five faculties do not exist within the five consciousnesses; by this analogy, [the characteristic of the object] does not exist within the five consciousnesses.

Regarding the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*): because those atoms reach the limit of the most subtle form-and-name (*nāmarūpa*), they are beyond the power of the visual consciousness and other cognitions to confront.
Therefore, it is said that while atoms serve as the causal condition for the arising of consciousness, they do not constitute an objective referent (*ālambana*).

Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya): it refers to the cognizing consciousness that arises bearing the aspect of that [object], and which possesses substantial reality, such that the cognizing consciousness relies upon it for its arising.
Even if atoms of form and so forth possessed substantial reality and could produce the five sensory consciousnesses, they would still potentially possess the status of being an object.

However, it is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just as the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth are not objects for the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and so forth, because they lack the appearance of those [objects].
Likewise, atoms (*paramāṇu*) do not possess the status of being an object of cognition for the visual consciousness and so forth.

I shall now explain the verses. First, I will clarify the correct meaning of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). "The cognizing consciousness arises bearing the aspect of that [object]" explains that there is an objective sphere which serves as the object.
"And it possesses substantial reality, causing the cognizing consciousness to arise by depending upon it" explains that there is a condition for the arising of consciousness.
This is because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), which is the subject that cognizes, and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which is the object of cognition, both depend upon the same [basis].

The self-verifying portion (svasaṃvittibhāga) arises; because it arises simultaneously with [the object-cognizing portion], neither preceding nor following it, one should know that consciousness does not arise from itself.

Its arising necessarily involves a mental aspect (nimitta) as its objective referent (ālambana). That aspect does not arise independently; its arising necessarily induces consciousness to function as the subjective cognizer (ālambaka-citta).
By means of this single factor, there are two functions: first, it can induce consciousness; second, it acts as an object-condition (*ālambana*).

Therefore, it is called an "object-condition" (*ālambana*) and is also termed a "condition" (*pratyaya*). Regarding the passage beginning with "matter and so forth," this is the formal explanation of the verse. As for the statement "the atoms of matter and so forth...

yet they are not the object-condition," this explains the thesis established by the first two lines [of the verse]. This is similar to the case of the eye-faculty and so forth, up to the point where "that [consciousness] does not exist."
Regarding "by way of characteristics": this explains the meaning of the cause and the analogy in the latter two phrases.

As for "thus, the atom reaches the point where there is no object of cognition," this concludes by clarifying that while the sense of an object of cognition may be conceptually possible, there is necessarily no objective realm to be cognized.
"Conjoined with the five consciousnesses, even if there is an object that is not a causal condition, its substance is truly non-existent, like a second moon.

This is the formal argument (prayoga) established by the Master [Dharmakīrti] to refute the meaning of the second position. "Conjoined" is the subject (dharmin) of the prior thesis; it refers to [the object] in relation to the five consciousnesses.

If one proposes as a thesis that the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not a causal condition (*pratyaya*), the reason (*hetu*) is that its substance is non-existent, and the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*) is like a second moon.

This refers to the "composite phenomena" (*saṃghāta-dharma*) which they grasp; because their characteristic is a collection and they manifest as forms and colors, they are said to be "existent objects.
Even if one were to concede that there is an object of cognition within the five consciousnesses, it would not be that which gives rise to the consciousness.
This is the condition [for the appearance of the object]. Because that composite entity lacks substantial reality, it is like a second moon; for that appears erroneously due to pressing on the eye.

This serves as a metaphor to show that the composite is fundamentally not truly existent. Since it is merely a collection of atoms where a conventional characteristic arises, it is said that even if one were to grant that there is an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it does not possess the meaning of being a causal condition (*pratyaya*).

The aggregation of form and other factors [occurs] in relation to visual consciousness and the rest because they possess those characteristics; thus, even if it were made an object of cognition (*ālambana*), it lacks the actual meaning of being an object.

Just as when the eyes are disordered one sees a second moon, which has no substantial reality and cannot produce [cognition], so too this aggregation in relation to visual consciousness and the rest lacks the meaning of being an object.
This explains the meaning of the preceding verse. It refers to the grasping of the composite characteristics of form and so forth within visual consciousness and the like.

Even if one were to grant that those composite characteristics appear and thus constitute an object of perception (*ālambana*), the composite itself lacks substantial reality and therefore lacks the status of being a causal condition (*ālambana-artha*).
This is like seeing a second moon in the eye due to a visual disorder; that second moon does not truly exist. Because...
The analogy of the combination is likewise not substantially existent; it cannot produce consciousness, and therefore lacks the status of an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Thus, regarding the object-condition, both external factors lack one essential element and are consequently untenable.

This establishes that the two positions previously maintained are irrational. Regarding the "two external things": these refer to the atoms (*paramāṇu*) as previously asserted, which are held to exist separately from their distinct characteristics;
hence they are called "external things. As for the mutual deficiency of one factor regarding the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*):

this means that with respect to the atoms, there is a deficiency of the objective object (*ālambana-viṣaya*), and with respect to their aggregation, there is a deficiency of the condition for the arising of consciousness. Therefore, these two external things [are deficient].
Both [positions] are unreasonable. The Commentary states: "Apart from consciousness, one clings to two kinds of atoms (paramāṇu) as a collective aggregate;

however, these both lack one of the two required factors. For an object to be a cognitive support (ālambana), it must possess both the manifestation of its own essential characteristic (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) and the capacity to produce [consciousness].
In the case of atoms, the first factor (the aforementioned manifestation of their own essential characteristic) is lacking. Regarding the second...
[The term] "penetrating" (tōng) means that the second [factor]—namely, both the preceding [condition] and the nature of being able to produce—is thereby eliminated.

If this is the case, then the two kinds of faults discussed above are once again gathered together and rectified so as to be without error. The *Lun shi ji* (Record of the Commentary on the Treatise) states: "This is merely a warning not to commit such errors."
Some maintain that form and other [sensory objects] each possess multiple characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Among these, one portion constitutes the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, the atoms (*paramāṇu*) support one another such that each possesses a single characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*). This characteristic is substantially existent and is capable of producing a cognition that resembles its own characteristic.
Therefore, it acts as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.

Because the previous master [Vasubandhu] admitted that atoms (*paramāṇu*) can produce consciousness at the level of the ultimate particle, while admitting they act as the object-condition at the level of the composite (*saṃghāta*), other schools subsequently argued:
"Previously, you admitted that atoms possess the condition for producing consciousness, and you also admitted the composite."
It serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*). Now, it is inferred that within the substance of an atom (*paramāṇu*) there exists the sense of aggregation;

therefore, atoms possess the characteristic of combination. Thus, when atoms are able to induce the arising of consciousness, their substance—being endowed with aggregation—acts as the objective condition.

Both meanings are thus fully provided; there can certainly be no error. When it is now said that "there are those who grasp at form (*rūpa*) and so forth," the phrase "and so forth" refers to the five sense objects:
sound, odor, taste, and touch. Regarding the statement that "each has many characteristics": this means that form possesses characteristics such as blue and yellow;

sound possesses characteristics such as clear and dull; odor possesses characteristics such as pleasant and unpleasant; taste possesses characteristics such as sweet and bitter; and touch possesses [characteristics such as] cold...

Regarding the characteristics of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, that which constitutes a portion of their objective domain through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) refers to the fact that within the substantial entities of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the five sense objects,
each possesses a portion of collective aggregation (*saṃcita*). Therefore, because these portions are present as objects of direct perception, all the atoms—
by virtue of possessing this collective aggregation within their substance— mutually support one another, such that each atom has a portion within the five sense objects.
The appearance of a composite aggregate is real; each [atom] is capable of producing a cognition that resembles its own form.
This explains that the substance of the atom possesses a composite state, which can serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses.
This too is irrational. Why?

Because the collection [of atoms], like hardness and so forth, is admitted to be a condition for visual consciousness and the rest, but not their object, since it possesses the characteristics of an atom.
The author of the treatise further establishes an inference (*anumāna*) to refute that counter-argument. "Aggregation" is the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition;

"it is a condition for visual consciousness and so forth, yet it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*)" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Because it is admitted to possess the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*)" is the reason (*hetu*).

"Just like solidity and so forth" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This means that the essence of the atoms as conceived by the opponent—which possesses the characteristic of aggregation—is just like solidity, moisture, and so on.
The characteristics of heat, motion, and so forth are not visible to the eye; they lack the status of being objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Therefore, the thesis is established as follows:

Even if it were granted that these are conditions for the arising of visual and other consciousnesses, they do not possess the nature of being objects of cognition, because it is granted that the essence of atoms (*paramāṇu*) consists of a collection of aggregations, and that this is fundamentally the single characteristic of the atom itself.

Just as characteristics such as solidity, although they exist substantially, may be objects of cognition for visual consciousness and other sensory cognitions, yet they are not its *ālambana* (objective referents), because those characteristics do not exist within the visual consciousness itself;
the same principle should apply to the characteristics of the aggregation of atoms, such as form and so forth.
Because both [schools] maintain that these are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of atoms (*paramāṇu*), this explains the meaning of the preceding verse.

Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are the natures (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); earth, water, fire, and wind are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the four great elements.

Since solidity and the others are able to produce [the elements], while earth and the others only manifest [as a result], it is known that the characteristic forms of the natures—solidity and so forth—are real.
There is a substance that, in relation to the visual and other consciousnesses, may possess the status of being an object (*ālambana-artha*), yet it is not the actual objective referent (*ālambana*).

This is because within the visual and other consciousnesses, there is no nature of characteristics such as solidity and so forth. This is because solidity, moisture, and the like exist only in their state as substances (*bhāva-avasthā*), and do not manifest with the same appearances as earth and the other elements.
Below the section on form (*rūpa*), the argument applies the analogy to the dharma: namely, that the substance of an atom does not possess a composite [nature].
The collection (*saṃcita*) is admitted to be substantially existent and capable of serving as a condition; however, it is not an object-condition (*ālambana*).

This is because within visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, there is no entity of atoms (*paramāṇu*) that possesses the characteristic of a collective aggregate. Therefore, it is said to be "likewise. This is due to the adherence to the view that the aggregate is not separate from the atoms.

Therefore, he further rebukes them, saying: "Since they both maintain that atoms possess such characteristics, they must hold that the visual and other consciousnesses are able to take atoms as their objects; yet these aggregated characteristics arise separately [from the atoms]."

Based on the preceding [argument], they further maintain that the nature of the atom (*paramāṇu*) possesses the characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*), which serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

The Master refutes this with the analogy of hardness and so forth, stating that because what they grasp is in both cases the very nature of the atomic form, it lacks the status of an objective condition.
Consequently, they again maintain that the characteristic of aggregation is itself the atom, because its form manifests.
There exists such an object of cognition whose substance is that of atoms (*paramāṇu*), and which is further capable of producing consciousness.
When it is now said that the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth can take as their objects the various characteristics of aggregated atoms, this refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

The characteristics of these aggregations all have the combination and accumulation of atoms as their substance; because this substance is capable of producing consciousness, [the consciousness] takes those atoms and their aggregated distinctions as its object.

Regarding the characteristic (*nimitta*): it is further able to induce the production of differentiated consciousnesses because consciousness arises appearing as objects. Therefore, it is said that there is a further distinct production of the characteristics of the cognition of jars, bowls, and so forth.
If one were to hold [the view] that these are not distinct, then they would have no distinction; yet they are not distinct merely because their shapes are different.
Because the distinction of shape is not real, the Master of the Treatise speaks this verse to refute the meaning of the preceding attachment. The first line restates that attachment:

they claim that since the shapes of objects such as jars and bowls are distinct, the characteristics of the cognitions produced by them are likewise distinct. The second line provides a general refutation, stating that [the cognition] has an object of perception (*ālambana*).

Although there is a distinction between a jar and a bowl, the characteristic of the cognition that apprehends them should not differ, because it is previously asserted that only atoms can produce consciousness.
The latter two lines explain this point: namely, since the shapes of the jar and the bowl are not substantially real.

It cannot induce the arising of a cognitive aspect that perceives form; therefore it is said: "Because form is not distinct, the cognitive aspect is also not distinct," since that distinction of form does not exist as a reality.

Regarding objects such as jars and bowls, their large or small dimensions are established by the number of atoms that constitute them; since this quantity is identical, the corresponding cognitions of them would likewise be without distinction.
If it is argued that the cognitions differ because the shapes and physical characteristics of those objects differ, this reasoning is also incorrect.
The distinct shapes of jars and so forth exist only upon conventional phenomena such as pots; they do not belong to the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). This explains the meaning of the preceding verse.
"Jars, bowls, and so forth" refers to the multiplicity of objects; "large, small, and so forth" refers to the distinctions among shapes.

This explains that there are differences in the objective referents (*ālambana*). As for the statement that "the number of the ultimate atoms capable of constituting them is the same," it means [they are equal] in terms of their plurality.

The capacity to produce a large [cognition] is small [in its cause]; the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) are fundamentally identical. This explains that there is no distinction in the conditions for the arising of consciousness.

Regarding the statement that "there is no distinction in the corresponding cognition of those conditions," they maintain that the aggregate (*saṃcita*) serves as the object; thus, it is from the ultimate atoms that consciousness arises.
Since the atoms are identical, the characteristics of the cognition produced by them should likewise be without distinction. The phrase "If one says...
(referring to the following) restates the opponent's position to serve as the refutation for the third line; therefore, it states, "In principle, this is also not so. The phrase "The jar, etc.

explains the fourth line, thereby establishing the meaning of the preceding third line. The character *huáng* (瓨) is pronounced *gāng*; it refers to a long-necked bottle. The translator [uses this term]...
The two terms "jar" (ghaṭa) and "bottle" (kalaśa) are used interchangeably.
One should not maintain that even atoms possess distinct shapes. Why is this? Because the magnitude of atoms is equal;
distinctions of shape exist only conventionally, for when [an object] is analyzed down to its ultimate atoms, [no such distinction remains].

Because he has attained equanimity through meditative concentration, there is a fear that he might further argue that atoms also possess distinct shapes and forms; therefore, [the author] first suppresses this by saying, "That should not be so," and so forth. Why is this?
It is to interrogate and explain the meaning of the non-distinctness of atoms. The first line of the verse refers to that which is capable of...
They constitute atoms (*paramāṇu*). Whichever number there may be, their magnitude is equal, as there is no distinction between them.
The second phrase refutes the notion that those distinct shapes are merely conventional designations and cannot produce cognition. The final two phrases explain and establish the preceding phrase:
that is to say, when those shapes are analyzed down to the level of atoms, the cognitive appearance (*buddhi-lakṣaṇa*) produced by perceiving those distinct shapes is necessarily abandoned.

It is not the case that jars, bowls, and the like can constitute atoms; since they possess distinct dimensions and forms, they must relinquish their subtle, spherical characteristics. Thus, one knows that distinct shapes exist only conventionally and are not real.

Furthermore, when a distinct object possessing shape is analyzed down to the level of atoms, the cognition of that shape is necessarily abandoned, whereas this is not the case for substances such as blue and so forth.

When analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), that cognition can be abandoned. Therefore, because of these distinctions of shape, they exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛti-sat*) and do not reside in real entities (*dravya*) like blue and so forth.
Thus, it is thoroughly established by reason that the nature of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses is not external form and the like.
This explains the meaning of the preceding verse. It means that it is not the case that jars and bowls possess distinct physical dimensions;

rather, they must relinquish the characteristics of the complete atoms (*paramāṇu*) that constitute them, because those atoms are devoid of transformation. Thus, one knows that distinct shapes exist only conventionally and are not real.
This explains the middle line. Furthermore, "if a distinct object with shape is analyzed down to its atoms, the cognition of it is necessarily abandoned," explains the final line.

Two points: regarding those things that are not blue or other such [colors], where the cognition of them can be discarded when analyzed down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), this serves as an illustrative example.

That is to say, while shape (*saṃsthāna*) may still be further analyzed, color (*varṇa*) cannot be divided. Since it can be further analyzed, one should know that shape is conventional (*prajñapti*); since it cannot be divided, color is real.

It also exists as a substantial entity. Therefore, [the author] concludes below by demonstrating that internal form serves as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); this principle is thoroughly established.
How could that object-condition not exist at all? It is certainly not non-existent. If that is so, how is it [present]?

Internal matter appears as if external; it serves as the objective condition for consciousness. This is accepted because its aspect exists within consciousness and because it can produce consciousness.
Previously, the error of the externalist attachment was refuted; here, it is clarified that internal matter is the correct [condition]. Therefore, he asks again: "Those first five..."

[Question: Is it not the case that the dharmas which serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness do not exist at all? [Answer: It is not that they do not exist at all. [Question: If so, what is the meaning of this? [Response:

This restates and inquires into the sense of "not non-existent at all. In the verse, a thesis (*pakṣa*) is established based on internal form (*rūpa*), demonstrating the meaning of the object-condition according to the Mahāyāna.
Internal form is the subject (*dharmin*) of the proposition; the thesis is that it serves as the object-condition for consciousness.
It is granted that those images reside within consciousness and serve as causes for the arising of consciousness, just as external appearances serve as metaphors.
The first two lines of the verse refer to the internal image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*); they appear as if there were dharmas existing outside the mind, just as [the opponent] clings to them.

It acts as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five sensory consciousnesses. The Commentary states: "In this context, the term 'internal' is used to show that the object of cognition does not exist apart from consciousness.
Because worldly convention collectively accepts that objects abide externally, one might think they are like external things;

however, since these do not exist apart from consciousness, it should be understood that form has no internal or external existence—it is the grasper who perceives them as external. This is said in contrast to [the view of] those who hold [to such externality].

Because there is the external, there is also the name "internal. If one does not grasp at the external, then even the internal cannot be named. When both internal and external are extinguished, the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established.

The latter two phrases explain, in order, the meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*). To allow that its aspect (*nimitta*) exists within consciousness is the sense of "having an object" (*sālambana*).
And because it can produce consciousness, it has the sense of being a "condition" (*pratyaya*).
Although external objects do not exist, there is internal form that appears as if it were an external object, serving as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
It is accepted that visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing the aspect of those [objects] and are produced from them, because they possess these two characteristics.
"Although external objects do not exist" refers to the prior refutation of the logical impossibility of atoms being either discrete or aggregated.
"Yet there is internal form that appears as if it were an external object, serving as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)" explains the first two lines of the verse.
"Admitting that visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing the aspect of those [objects] and are produced from them" explains the latter two lines. "Arising bearing their aspect" means:
The term "object-condition" (*ālambana*) is explained by its meaning of being that from which [cognition] arises; thus, it is said to possess two meanings.
Since this internal objective aspect is not separate from consciousness, how can it arise simultaneously with consciousness and yet function as its condition?

The proponents of other vehicles ask: "If the internal objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) does not depart from consciousness and arises simultaneously with it, how can that which arises simultaneously serve as a condition for consciousness?
For what reason? It is necessary that the former induces the latter before the sense of being a 'condition' (ālambana) can exist."
Because they are necessarily concomitant, they also act as conditions simultaneously; or rather, because the former acts as a condition for the latter by inducing its functional capacity.
The Master replies: "The object and consciousness are necessarily concomitant; although they arise simultaneously, they are nonetheless able to act as conditions."
It induces consciousness. If it does not induce it, it cannot be said to arise simultaneously or to function as a concomitant.

The latter two phrases answer the question regarding the sequence of priority and posteriority: that is, either the functional capacity of the preceding consciousness acts as the condition for inducing the subsequent consciousness;
just as the eye conditions form, the functional capacity within that form induces the consciousness to arise together with it, and the consciousness then conditions [the subsequent state].

Regarding form: when the preceding visual consciousness ceases and the subsequent consciousness arises, it is also the functional capacity that induces the preceding consciousness which is able to induce the subsequent consciousness to apprehend its object.

Therefore, it is said that the former serves as the condition for the latter; because it is this functional capacity that draws forth the arising of that consciousness, [the former is called a condition].
Because the objective aspect (*viṣaya-ākāra*) and consciousness necessarily accompany one another, even though they arise simultaneously, the former still acts as a condition for the latter.

Proponents of the theory of light (*prakāśavādin*) state that if two things follow one another in their presence or absence, they may possess the relationship of cause and effect despite being produced at the same time.

Alternatively, the aspect of a preceding consciousness serves as the condition for a subsequent consciousness, inducing the arising of a capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that produces an appearance resembling its own fruit;
this does not contradict reason.

Regarding the phrase "the aspect of the object" (*viṣayākāra*), the first two lines of the verse are explained. Regarding the phrase "in the *Hetuvidyā*," a scriptural proof is cited, which states: "If..."
This objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and that subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are concomitant in their presence or absence;

although they arise simultaneously, it is nonetheless possible for the objective aspect to function as the cause and the subjective aspect as the effect. Regarding the phrase "concomitant in presence or absence":

"presence" refers to the time when the two divisions of objective and subjective aspects abide in the state of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), while "absence" refers to the time when the two divisions of objective and subjective aspects abide in the state of seeds (*bīja*). Abiding in...
At the time of functioning, those respective functions exist; within the state of the seeds, those respective functions do not exist.

This explains that the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), whether manifest or as seeds, are invariably concomitant; this is the meaning of "not being separate. Alternatively, the preceding section explains the latter two lines:
the "root consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness. "Resembling its own fruit" means, for example, that the eye-faculty induces the production of the eye-consciousness.
When the body-faculty induces the arising of body-consciousness, it is termed its "own fruit. Thus, with the eyes and so forth as causes, consciousness arises as the fruit.
This means that that which induces within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) something resembling its own fruit is brought about by the functional power of the five faculties;
this does not contradict reason.
If the five consciousnesses arise by taking only internal form as their object, how can it also be said that the eye and so forth serve as their conditions?

The followers of other vehicles ask: "If the five consciousnesses arise by taking only internal form as their object, how is it that they are described elsewhere [as being conditioned by the external]?"
It is also taught that consciousness arises only when the five faculties, such as the eye, serve as conditions.
The capacity for color within consciousness is appropriately termed the "five faculties. This capacity and the objective color have functioned as mutual causes since beginningless time.

The Master of the Treatise replies: The first two phrases clarify that both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) belong to the category of form (*rūpa*). Therefore, when the term "form" is mentioned, both the faculty and its object are indicated.

This means that upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there exists the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) which is form; that which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) for the five sensory consciousnesses is termed the "five dust-like objects" (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The functional capacity within form that induces the five consciousnesses is termed the "five faculties. This accords with correct reasoning. The latter two lines clarify their mutual causality;
that is, the functional capacity of the five faculties and the form of the five objects have served as causes for one another since beginningless time.
The functional capacity acts as the cause that induces the objective forms, while the objective forms act as the cause that gives rise to the functional capacity. This is...
Regarding the meaning of mutual causality:

since consciousness can be produced, one infers the existence of the sense faculties (*indriya*) through analogy; these are merely functional capacities and are not externally constructed. Therefore, they reside upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

It is not unreasonable to name the functional capacities regarding the five colors as the "eye-faculties" and so forth, because there is no logical distinction between a capacity and that which gives rise to consciousness.

Although it cannot be definitively stated whether [the faculty] resides in the consciousness or elsewhere, since external phenomena do not exist according to reason, one must certainly admit this [position].
It resides in consciousness and nowhere else; this is the function of the faculty. This faculty and the objective form have served as reciprocal causes since beginningless time.
That is to say, when this faculty reaches its state of maturation, it gives rise to the five internal objective forms upon the manifest consciousness. These internal objective forms—
Furthermore, it can also give rise to the functional capacities of the five sense organs within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

As for whether these two types of form—the organs and their objects—are identical to or different from the consciousness, or neither identical nor different, one should explain this according to one's preference. Thus, all these consciousnesses have only the internal aspects of objects as their objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This is well-established by reasoning.

Since the existence of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is known through inference based on the arising of consciousness, it follows that the faculties are not objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but are knowable only through inference (*anumāna*).

Furthermore, these faculties are merely functional capacities and are not produced from external [elements], because the faculties and their objects do not occupy the same location when consciousness arises.

The faculties are called the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), which are the five sense organs. The objects of perception are called the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), which are the five sensory objects (*viṣaya*).
Because they are produced externally, they carry the meaning of "objects" (*viṣaya*). Therefore, in the main text below, the first two lines are correctly explained.
"Because there is no distinction in principle regarding the capacity to produce consciousness" means that the capacity to produce consciousness is termed the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate faculty).
Taking only that which produces consciousness as being the faculty itself involves no further meaning.

"Whether it resides in consciousness or elsewhere, though it cannot be said" means that form (*rūpa*) not being separate from consciousness is called "residing in consciousness," while the existence of dharmas external to the mind is called "residing elsewhere. It is not [the case that]... [it is not so].
In discussing internal and external forms (*rūpa*), only those that give rise to consciousness are termed "ultimate sense faculties" (*paramārtha-indriya*). Therefore, it is said:

although they cannot be described [as substantial entities], one clings to the existence of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and their combinations as phenomena external to the mind. When analyzed through reasoning, since these are not truly existent, one must certainly admit this:
the form that gives rise to consciousness exists within consciousness and nothing else. Below this section on the faculties, the latter two [points] are explained.
[This] sentence—meaning, from here below—explains the sense of being successively causes for one another.

"The stage of maturation" refers to the stage when this retribution has already matured. That is to say, by means of the functional capacity of the five faculties, within the state of retribution, the five internal objects arise upon the substance of the manifest consciousness;
these are termed the "form of the object-part" (*nimitta-bhāga-rūpa*). From these internal objects, one is further able to give rise to the future...
The functional capacity of the five faculties (*indriya*) upon which the resultant maturation (*vipākaphala*) arises is called the "ultimate faculty" (*paramārthendriya*).

As for the previous statement that they are "externally derived" and the current statement that they are "internal objective forms" (*antarviṣaya-rūpa*): the former refers to them as externally derived because they were categorized as faculties and objects; the latter refers to them as internal objects because they are not separate from consciousness.

The Commentary states: "In this context, the term 'internal' means not being separate from consciousness. Since there is no 'external' in the first place, [the question arises: with respect to what [is it internal]?"

This constitutes the internal. Thus, we know that the designations "internal" and "external" are provisionally established according to conventional sentiment. Below the section on the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is revealed:

namely, that the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness consists of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), which are identical with the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

Therefore, they are called "one. Since matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are distinct from one another, they are also called "different. Being identical in essence while distinct in function, they are called "not one"; being distinct in function while identical in essence, they are [called "not different"].

It is also called "not different. One should explain this according to one's inclination based on a thorough realization of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If one does not thoroughly realize this, one will fall into error by following mere sensory contact.
Thus, the conclusion below demonstrates that internal form (*antar-rūpa*) is established as a logically sound objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

This is intended to refute the false attachments of other vehicles who hold that the conjunction of external atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitutes the objective condition; both [of those views] are irrational.
Commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (End)
